overview: This two-page strictly confidential despatch from the U.S. Embassy in Santiago reports an unconfirmed rumor that three Japanese merchant ships, escorted by heavy naval vessels, would soon reach Valparaíso. Embassy inquiries found no entry for the ships in the customs house’s confidential register and cast doubt on an anonymous telephone request to reserve dock space, although information obtained by the American consul suggested that a Japanese commercial representative named Kanamori claimed such a convoy was imminent and intended partly as a demonstration against United States power in the Pacific.

people.name: Claude G. Bowers
people.role: Sender of the U.S. Embassy despatch

people.name: Kanamori
people.role: Japanese representative of Itoh y Cia.; identification described as approximate

subfiles.title: Despatch on rumored arrival of convoyed Japanese merchant vessels at Valparaíso
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: Reports and evaluates an unconfirmed rumor that three Japanese merchant ships under heavy naval escort would soon arrive at Valparaíso.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy investigated reports that dock space had been reserved for three Japanese merchant vessels and found neither confirming entries in the customs house’s confidential register nor a credible source for the anonymous telephone request. The mission’s naval attaché likewise reported that the rumor could not be confirmed. A memorandum from the American consul nevertheless recorded Kanamori’s alleged assertion that a Japanese convoy was coming, protected by heavy ships, to deliver goods and undermine confidence in United States control of the Pacific. The consul was instructed to report any additional information.

interest: The despatch is useful for studying how U.S. diplomats assessed maritime intelligence and commercial rumors in Latin America during the Pacific War. Particularly revealing is the combination of skeptical verification—checking port records and questioning the logistics of the alleged reservation—with human intelligence obtained by a bank employee posing as an Axis sympathizer. The reported claim that the voyage was intended to weaken Latin American confidence in U.S. naval supremacy also illuminates contemporary fears about Japanese economic activity as wartime psychological warfare.
